speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of a report I have just received, concerning which therefore I have not been able to give him notice. If he prefers to take this question as notice and answer it at a subsequent time it will be, of course, quite understandable. My question is, has the Prime Minister any comment to make on the statement of the United Kingdom Prime Minister in the House of Commons in London today to the effect that he is calling on the west to study the possibility of a partial pull-back or disengagement from central Europe in the interests of the prevention of war?

subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED STATEMENT BY U.K. PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that matter has not been brought to my attention, and I shall take it as notice.
Mr. Speaker, I might refer as well to one other matter in connection with discussions which are taking place at the present time. As the house knows, the Soviet government delivered notes to the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and France on March 2 relating to the possibility of negotiations taking place on problems relating to Germany. On the same date a note was addressed to the Canadian government by the Soviet union. This was in reply to the Canadian note of February 17, which was tabled on the same day by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The note addressed to Canada does not contain anything of significance that is not to be found in the notes addressed to the United Kingdom, the United States and France. Consultations among NATO governments and in the NATO council are now in progress, and naturally any matters such as the one referred to by the hon. gentleman would receive that consideration by the NATO council.
The house will, of course, be aware of the fact that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom is planning to visit Washington later this month, I think around the 15th or 16th. The matter of having an invitation extended to Mr. Macmillan, which invitation has always been an open one in any event, has

been discussed informally with the United Kingdom high commissioner, and I have today sent Mr. Macmillan a message expressing the hope that following his visit to Washington he will come to Ottawa to consult here with the members of the government and, I might add, the hope that consideration might be given to his addressing both houses on that occasion.

In addition to this cost it is estimated that the federal government will have paid for constructing the highway through the national parks approximately $61 million. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is made necessary because of the need for additional money in order to proceed with the completion of the trans-Canada highway program in the nine provinces to which the program applies. This project, I suggest, is an example of the kind of leadership which can be provided by the federal government with regard to an important national development. Though from time to time the federal government may embark on projects which do not immediately receive the full or unanimous support of the provinces of this country, nevertheless I think in the light of its experience the government will agree that in almost every instance in which the federal government has endeavoured to enact, with the co-operation of the provinces, legislation designed to improve the lot of Canadians the provinces generally have been most cooperative.
Nine provinces are engaged in this project. Some have made more progress toward the completion of the highway than others. There
[Mr. Green.l
is one province, the province of Quebec, which has not seen fit to take advantage of this measure. Premier Duplessis in his own good judgment has decided that this project should not apply to the province of Quebec.
I would think that the people of Quebec are in as great need of good highways, and deserve them as much, as people in any other part of this country, and I believe from my study of this problem that the premier of Quebec has fallen into great error by refusing to co-operate with the federal government in this field. It is an error which I suppose does not impose any real hardship or suffering or inconvenience upon the premier of the province, but I am certain in my mind that it withholds from the people of Quebec a very important service and a very important right, namely the presence in their province of a part of the trans-Canada highway built to the standard which has been set for this highway and, what is equally important, the advantage of having money contributed from the national treasury for this purpose. I would suggest that the premier of Quebec has allowed his ancient quarrel with the federal government to deprive the people of that province of a very important service, a project which is national in character and which will serve the people of this country well.
I think the present government has made an error in the opposite direction. Progress has been made toward the completion of this project in many of the provinces. The western provinces are making great progress. Saskatchewan has completed its project; Manitoba and Alberta have announced that their highway is almost completed.
I asked earlier, when we were discussing the resolution, what if any consideration the government had given to the expansion of this very important undertaking. I suggest that within the scope of the trans-Canada highway there is room for expansion. There is room for the second trans-Canada highway project that we have heard so much about. I submit to the government that it is time this very important undertaking should be extended into a national highways program to meet needs of Canadians generally, and that the government should undertake such a program in co-operation with the provinces.
As a good Canadian citizen, I do not believe that in this field we should be 40 years behind the United States. There is no reason why we in Canada, when we have the manpower and the resources available, should be satisfied with one project, important though it is. We should go ahead at this moment, this year, to provide an extension of this legislation to meet the highway needs of the people of this country.

There is another very important reason why, I submit, now is the time for such a development. We have heard about the government's winter work program. We were told the other day that as far as on-site work is concerned, employment is now being provided for more than 30,000 Canadians. What will happen to the 30,000 people who are employed on the winter work program when their employment ceases? Are these people to be added to the unemployment rolls during the summer months? In the early years of the trans-Canada highway project, when we asked for an extension we were told by the government of the day that our resources were fully employed, that we had no more manpower available for such an expansion and that, desirable though it might be, our resources should not be used in that direction.
That argument cannot be used today. We have a tremendous surplus of idle manpower, men anxious to be engaged in useful work. We have the material resources that are required for a great advance in this project, and I would suggest that now is the time for this government to show leadership in the provision of adequate highways and in the provision of a program that will help deal with the vexed question of unemployment.
I asked this question earlier and I repeat it now. Has the minister within his department, or has the Department of Labour or any other department of the government, undertaken a survey to see how an expanded highway program could be used to help reduce the large number of unemployed in Canada at this time? I believe that the government is very concerned about the unemployment problem, and indeed any government that accepts its responsibilities in this day and age must be concerned with problems of this magnitude. I would suggest that one of the obvious things the government could do would be to undertake a survey of the great public works projects that might be instituted to put people to work.
I ask the minister whether there has been any survey as to what effect an expanded highway program for either a second trans-Canada highway or highways of this standard or any other standard running north and south would produce. Has there been any encouragement given to the provinces and municipalities by the federal government to undertake this kind of road development? I suggest that this kind of leadership is required at the present time more than at any other time in recent years because of the financial difficulties that are being faced by the provinces and municipalities.
Trans-Canada Highway Act
It is no secret that provincial finances are more difficult now than they have been in the last several years. The same is true of municipal finances. The difficulty of raising municipal and provincial budgets for their important works programs is becoming more and more acute. Are the minister and the government prepared to allow these difficulties to grow? Are they prepared to have it become increasingly difficult for provinces and municipalities to meet the problem of providing adequate road facilities for the public? These remarks could also be extended to include urban areas. The provision of roads through the great cities of our country taxes the financial resources of those cities.
We urge the minister to have a comprehensive study made of this question to see how a program of this kind could be utilized in 1959 to help solve the question of unemployment. There are provinces that are ready to embark on such a program. The province of Saskatchewan has been urging the government to co-operate in just such a project. As I pointed out on a previous occasion, the estimated labour content in building the trans-Canada highway in that province was 27 per cent. I suggest that is a high labour content. This is the kind of project which if extended would provide substantial employment in Canada at this time.
I express the hope that the minister will tell the house what study the government has given to this problem and what study it has made concerning how such a project could fit in with a program designed to put people to work, and what the government intend to do by way of action in the days ahead.

It is not my responsibility, Mr. Speaker, to judge the matter on its merits. However, I feels its significance is such that it should not be turned into a political football. It is significant enough because it involves a principle of no mean value, a legal principle rooted in history, namely the principle of provincial autonomy.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not go into the details of the matter, but I would point out to all those who seek to discredit the government of the province of Quebec with regard to that particular matter of the trans-Canada highway,-and they should be examining the problem in the light of the principles which lie at the base of this juridical fact of provincial autonomy-that it is not merely a question of highways. It is a question of determining under what conditions the trans-Canada highway is to be built. The province of Quebec has on several occasions expressed her opinion on the subject through the provincial authorities, and more particularly last week, when the provincial minister of highways said what he had in mind, stating that provincial autonomy is involved in the building of that highway and that the government of the province of Quebec cannot, at this time, accept to take any part in this project because, he said, the conditions set by the Ottawa government are


not in accordance with the sovereign policy of the province.
To my mind, this is the only standpoint from which the problem must be faced.
I think, moreover, that the provincial government of Quebec has, until now, made some considerable effort to provide the people of the province of Quebec with an adequate network of roads, so that no one need accuse it of all sorts of partisan and small-minded intentions with regard to the matter.
A few moments ago, in this debate, I heard a C.C.F. member say,-as I understood it,- that the province of Quebec does not need to improve its highway network and that Quebec people are perfectly satisfied with what they now have, as their government is refusing federal aid in this respect. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that we must in all fairness commend the provincial authorities of Quebec for having given our province an adequate road network. Considering the magnitude of this network and the considerable mileage involved, we have in the province of Quebec perfectly good roads-in fact excellent roads-that earn praises from tourists who visit the province. The project is, I think, not yet completed, as improvement work is continually being carried on and because this year's provincial budget for highways amounts to some $134 million. This shows, Mr. Speaker, how much importance the provincial government attaches to the highway problem.
In the past, some political opponents have taken the Quebec provincial government to task for spending too much money on highways. Yet, last week I heard them say in this house that Quebec's highway network is altogether inadequate, and that the roads are quite outdated.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be proper to consider the problem, to approach it in the only way it should be approached, from the angle of provincial political sovereignty. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the government consider the problem from the angle of provincial autonomy and consider the possibility of entering into arrangements which would not impose such conditions as are now being refused by the Quebec provincial government.
In closing, I again emphasize this aspect of the problem: this is not a matter of partisan politics, but one of basic principle and a vital one, since it was historically confirmed in 1867.

speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke of the intention to have this measure referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. However, before I so move, I think I should make a few comments.
The Veterans Rehabilitation Act has been the means of providing important rehabilitation aids to veterans of world war II and of the action in Korea. The principal benefits under the act have been of an educational nature and veterans have received vocational, technical, pre-matriculation and both undergraduate and post-graduate university training under the provisions of this act.
This training has proved of inestimable value to many veterans of whom more than 100,000 completed their courses. As the members of this committee know, the largest part of this training was given during the immediate post-war years. There are still, however, nearly sixty world war II veterans taking training, of whom over 40 are in university. There are about 25 veterans of the special force who served in Korea still pursuing their studies, of whom all except two or three are in university. There may possibly be a few who for reasons of illness may yet have courses made available to them.
Of the number now taking training some 20 are pensioners. The authority for the training of pensioners is contained both in section 15 of this act and in the pensioners training regulations authorized under the Department of Veterans Affairs Act. It is considered desirable from an administrative point of view that the authority for the training or retraining of pensioners should flow from one source. This bill accordingly proposes the repeal of section 15 of the act in order that the pensioners training regulations may in future be the sole authority for such training.

Veterans Rehabilitation Act
The act also authorizes the payment of allqwappes for tjie, purpose. of assisting veterans'during the progress of their training. It also provides for the payment of allowances while veterans are awaiting returns from a business venture. This now applies only to those who are participating in the benefits offered under the Veterans' Land Act. There were also allowances given to certain veterans who years ago were out of work or temporarily incapacitated.
: The bill proposes an amendment which, in a limited number of cases, would allow a refund to those veterans who had less than nine months university training and later made certain repayments in order to qualify under the Veterans' Land Act. Qualification under the latter act required the repayment of educational allowances and costs paid by the department. In some cases a veteran decided not to proceed with a contract under the Veterans' Land Act, or terminated his contract shortly after it was entered upon and received little benefit. This amendment will provide the refund to the veteran of the amount by which his repayment exceeds any benefits under the Veterans' Land Act. There is no new policy involved in this amendment. In the past the amount required for these refunds has been obtained by means of a special vote in the estimates. It is better that it be a statutory item as now proposed.
There are a number of administrative amendments proposed by the bill. Many of these are desirable because of provisions of the act which have now become obsolete as the conditions they were designed to meet no longer apply. I do not think it necessary to describe these amendments as there are no matters of policy involved.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS REPEALING AND REPLACING ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment which the minister has just introduced reminds us all very sharply of the swift passage of time. The legislation which this bill proposes to amend was enacted in December, 1945, on the unanimous recommendation of a sixty-member special committee on veterans affairs. It is to the great credit of the federal government that action was taken so early after the war to make provision for the re-establishment of Canadian veterans. As early as 1941, prior to the enactment of the present legislation which is now being amended, veterans rehabilitation benefits were set forth in a post-discharge re-establishment order in 1941, and in 1944 this was revised by order in council No. P.C.5210. The act now being amended sets forth in legislative form the benefits contained in that order in council. Briefly, those benefits included payments to veterans of allowances graduated in proportion to family needs under certain conditions.

Two of those allowances related, as the minister has pointed out, to unemployed veterans, to those who were unemployed because they were temporarily incapacitated, and to those who were able and willing, fo work but who were unable to find suitable jobs. The other provisions of the act had to do, as the minister has stated, with assisting veterans to establish themselves on farms and to provide them with vocational training and higher education and university training.
We welcome the amendment in tHis bill which will permit, reimbursement to those veterans who expended some, of. their own money, or agreed to forgo some of their credits with the 'intention of becoming Established on farms but who later were unable to take advantage of legislation designed for this purpose.
Today we are amending this legislation largely because the passage of time has made it no longer possible to apply the terms of this measure any further because there are no veterans who are now able , to take advantage of the provisions or to whom the sections of the legislation being repealed can apply. Canada has, therefore, implemented the principles of this legislation as far as humanly possible. In some respects this concludes a chapter in the history of veterans rehabilitation which, I think, will remain among the shining chapters of Canadian history.

The value of the original legislation with respect to veterans rehabilitation has been proved by experience in the return of veterans to civil life. I remember that when the legislation was discussed in the early days some doubts were raised in certain quarters that some who served for several years overseas and had been subjected to military life with all its vicissitudes and hazards would not respond very well to educational benefits or possibly for some time would not be capable of taking the fullest advantage of the educational benefits provided under this act. I believ'd that the - experience in the

administration of this act proved that the fears expressed in certain quarters were totally unjustified.
This measure is one of the most forwardlooking measures introduced in the House of Commons with respect to the rehabilitation of many of those who served this country. The experience with the legislation has laid a foundation that may be extended even into civilian aspects of life particularly with respect to federal assistance to education in terms of grants to universities and schools of higher learning.
I had the honour and privilege of serving with the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) on the committee that considered this legislation. The minister has explained to the house the new amendments that are being introduced to meet changing conditions and circumstances. speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-32, to amend the War Service Grants Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-32 is very much the same as the bill we have just had before the house. It is one of those bills referred to by previous speakers as having been par of the veterans' charter. It has served an excellent purpose for many years as far as veterans are concerned. It is my intention to recommend that this bill also be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs but before doing so I thought it appropriate to give a brief explanation of the intentions embodied in the bill and the effect of the amendments proposed.
The War Service Grants Act has been an important rehabilitation measure which has provided for the payment to veterans of world war II and of the action in Korea a war service gratuity based on length of service and payable in cash. It also introduced a new philosophy into veterans legislation which provided for the payment of a re-establishment credit devised to assist the economic rehabilitation of our veterans.
The ways in which this credit may he used are set forth in section 12 of the act where it, 66968-9-103
War Service Grants Act will be seen that credit is available for assistance in the securing and equipping of a home or business, for veterans insurance or as a factor leading to qualification under the Veterans' Land Act.
Over the years I have observed the importance of this credit in assisting materially in a practical way those veterans whose economic resources were limited. The payment of gratuity has been virtually completed but there are still a large number of veterans, well over 100,000, who have for various reasons such as family circumstances not applied for all their credits. There still remains some $18 million unpaid.
It has become evident that it would be unwise to limit too severely the time within which veterans may apply for the use of this remaining credit as we wish to make sure it will be used in the best possible way. For most world war II veterans there are only a few months left in which to use this credit. The bill therefore proposes that the time limit be extended for all world war II veterans to September 30, 1962, and veterans of the action in Korea would have until 15 years after the termination of their special force service in which to use the credit to which they are entitled.
This opportunity has been taken to propose other amendments. A number of these are of practical importance and some are of an administrative nature. The bill proposes, for example, to extend the use of re-establishment credit to permit the repair or modernization of a dwelling in which a single veteran resides with his dependent parent or parents. The department has observed that there are a number of single veterans who are not intending to marry and who have been living since the war in the family home which in many cases is owned by one or both of his parents. We have found that aside from their equity in the home the parents are dependent on the veteran for support. It is only right that such a veteran should he able to use his credit for the improvement of this dwelling. At present this is not permitted under the act. This amendment will therefore be of material assistance to these veterans.
There are a number of circumstances where re-establishment credit has not been used nor is it likely that it will ever be used under the present provisions of the act because of the mental illness of the veterans where recovery is unlikely before the end of the period during which credit is available. It is most desirable that the credit of such veterans should not be allowed to disappear because of these tragic circumstances. An amendment is accordingly proposed to make the unused credit of such a veteran available to his wife or dependent children. ...

War Service Grants Act
Hon. members are aware of the relationship between re-establishment credit and the benefits under the Veterans' Land Act and that these are alternate benefits which provide in different ways for the rehabilitation of veterans. Thus, a veteran who has used his re-establishment credit for the purposes set forth in the act is not able thereupon, in addition, to qualify for benefits under the Veterans' Land Act. It was not thought, however, that the use of re-establishment credit, perhaps prematurely, for other purposes should permanently deprive a veteran of eligibility under the Veterans' Land Act nor would it be equitable to allow him to enjoy both of these substantial benefits. The amendment therefore provides that on repayment of the used re-establishment credit he may then, if otherwise acceptable, qualify under the Veterans' Land Act. There have been instances arise where, following such repayment, the veteran changed his mind or did not proceed with the Veterans' Land Act, or he did proceed but the contract was soon terminated. He may thus have received no benefit or one smaller than his repayment. In the past, the excess of repayment over the benefit has been refunded to the veteran by means of a special vote in the estimates. An amendment now proposed would make this refund statutory.
At present the act provides that a veteran must qualify for benefits under the Veterans' Land Act by January 1, 1960. As the time within which re-establishment credit may be used is being extended by this bill it is evident that there should be a similar extension for the period within which a veteran may qualify for Veterans' Land Act benefits. Consequently it is proposed to extend this period also to September 30, 1962 for world war II veterans and for veterans of the action in Korea to 15 years after the termination of their service in the special force.
The remaining amendments are of an administrative nature. I think they are not of sufficient importance to require an explanation at this time.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side certainly welcome these amendments to the veterans rehabilitation act particularly those which will extend the time limit in which veterans can take advantage of their rehabilitation credits and of the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act. I am sure every hon. member was surprised, as I was, to hear that there were still $18 million in re-establishment credits available to veterans who had not yet applied for them.

As the minister pointed out, the original act, which was enacted in August, 1944, introduced a new philosophy of veterans reestablishment and rehabilitation and certainly was a great step forward in thinking as compared with what was done for veterans of the first world war. My colleagues who served in that war will remember that on discharge we were given, I think, a month's pay and allowances which was a sort of severance pay, plus a clothing allowance, and that was that. This new legislation went much farther in that it provided three separate cash payments to veterans. One payment was the war services gratuity, which was based on pay and allowances; the second was the rehabilitation grant, which was related to the period of service; and the third was the reestablishment credit.
Like other pieces of legislation, as the minister pointed out, this, too, was a part of the veterans' charter and was the result of the deliberations of a committee of the whole house which was anxious that no stone be left unturned to see that everything possible was done for our war veterans. In particular, it showed a sincere concern for the veteran himself, for his welfare and for the welfare of his family and dependants and a sincere desire to offset or minimize any financial loss of earning power that the veteran may have suffered because of his war service and to do everything possible to restore that earning power at least to the point he would have enjoyed had he not enlisted in the armed services.
As the minister pointed out, I am sure that this is the main amendment to this legislation. I refer to the extension of the time limit. The others have to do with extending the use of restablishment credits and with changes in administration. But I am sure we all hope that, as we are coming to the conclusion of the application and the extension of those benefits, there will never be again any future occasion for parliament to enact this kind of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of this group to express our wholehearted support for the proposal in this bill to amend the War Service Grants Act, but before proceeding with the few comments I wish to make I want to apologize sincerely for my off the cuff reply to an unseen member's voice on the government side respecting the percentage of this group who served in the armed forces of Canada. I did not in any way intend to offer any slight to hon. members who had not the opportunity to serve in the armed forces of Canada.

As the hon. member who has just taken his seat said, and as the minister mentioned, this legislation represents an important change in the outlook for rehabilitation legislation on behalf of veterans. We have established a completely new philosophy in that respect and I was very pleased to serve on the committee which dealt with this legislation during the war. I was surprised to hear that there was $18 million still unpaid in war services grants. Although it appears to be a large sum, it is indicative of the very large amount which has been paid out for war service grants over the years.
About $500 million.

I am pleased to hear that figure, Mr. Speaker, because it is some indication that parliament and the people of Canada have been willing to recognize in a substantial way in this legislation the services of the men who fought for freedom who, in my opinion, were the real freedom fighters. When I think of freedom fighters, I think of the men who fought on behalf of this country and in defence of freedom when freedom was being threatened by the nazi and fascist forces.
I am pleased to notice that the amendment provides for an extension of the time to the end of 1962 for world war II veterans and for Korean war veterans. I am very taken with the amendment which makes it possible for the veteran to use his credit to improve, repair or modernize his home. I am sure this is the result of the experience of the officials in administering the legislation of the country, and is another indication of the type of administration that veterans legislation has had in Canada throughout the years. There are no officials of any other department of government who are in closer touch with the human beings for whom they are administering legislation than the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Another thing which I am pleased with, and I am sure hon. members generally are also, is that amendment which provides for the credit to be used to the advantage of dependants and also the proposed amendment providing for an extension of the time to qualify for loans under the Veterans' Land Act. This is also another amendment which springs from the experience with the act and with the changing circumstances in the last year or two.
I am very pleased to know that the changes which to many members would appear to be inconsequential will provide advantages to those who would be denied them unless the amendment were passed. It will be a further recognition of the continuous consideration by members of all 66968-9-1031
War Service Grants Act parties in this house of the welfare of those who served this country in war.

War Service Grants Act try to see that these people got a little better consideration than seemed likely to be provided for them.

of the same amount and subject to the same conditions as he would have received had he been a member of the naval, military or air forces of Canada.

DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION Immigration branch-
52. Administration of the Immigration Act, $1,199,386.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on the immigration section of these estimates. I am certain the minister will understand that in some of the things I will say I am seeking answers to certain questions and an expression of opinion from the minister as to what she may have in mind with regard to changes in policies now that she has had the opportunity to spend quite a few months with the responsibilities which are hers.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend this point to the attention of the minister and ask what consideration has been given by her in particular and the department in general to the immigration policy of the department with respect to those who are rejected and not given any opportunity of knowing the reasons why they are rejected. I know that during the six years I have had the honour of being a member of this House of Commons I have listened to replies from three previous ministers. In my opinion, these replies were not at all satisfactory. I hope that a new approach is being considered by the present minister.
The reason I say those replies were completely unsatisfactory is because of my own knowledge that although it took a great many months to get final answers I did find that when a member of parliament took up the case of those who had made application for landing permits and were rejected, if he was persistent in following the case up it was eventually found that the information lodged with the overseas department of immigration was untrue. In one case the applicant had been turned down for 18 months because of something that was completely untrue. I am

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
reminded of one case in particular-and this did not occur while the present minister occupied her position-where an entire family came to Canada and one member was rejected. It took 18 months to find out why and then it was ascertained that a complaint had been lodged by a rejected suitor who maintained that this chap was a criminal. If the man could have known of the charge laid against him and who laid it, or at least the nature of the charge against him, the matter could have been settled very quickly. This is just one illustration.
I know that there are many arguments for and against this practice. It is not a right to come to Canada, it is a privilege. I should like to hear from the minister what her attitude is now compared with what her attitude was when she sat in opposition concerning the right to a hearing and the right of an applicant to know of any charges or implications against him. So far as I am concerned, because I feel very proud of what we call British justice, this is a matter of importance. I sincerely hope that she finds herself in a position, on this occasion when her estimates are before the committee, to be able to give us her views on this matter and also any changes that she may have in mind with relation to past policy.
There are one or two questions that I should like to ask and I only do so because I feel that now, after her months in office, the minister must have given some consideration to the Immigration Act itself and the regulations which are made under the authority of the act. I should like to ask the minister whether there are any indications of alterations in the act. I should like to mention only one or two points. May I ask the minister whether or not consideration has been given to the interpretation under the Immigration Act of the term "moral turpitude". The Immigration Act, section 5, paragraph (d) says:
persons who have been convicted of or admit having committed any crime involving moral turpitude-
These people are not eligible for admission. In looking at that in the first instance, I would say I completely agree. But, what is the interpretation of moral turpitude? I ask that because of a case which is now before the courts and to which I cannot refer because it is sub judice. However, from my own investigation I have ascertained certain things. A businessman who has a business in the United States and in Canada has been refused admittance under that section to carry on his business in Canada. The reason given was that he was found guilty in the United States seven or eight years ago on a charge of impaired driving, so he is ineligible
to enter Canada under that moral turpitude section. I do not know, but it just does not sound right to me. I do not know what the legal interpretation of the wording of that section is under the present administration.
May I, Mr. Chairman, go beyond that and speak about something about which I know the minister has always been sincere, and that is that there shall never be any second class citizens in Canada, and also that this idea shall be carried forward on a commonwealth basis in so far as immigration is concerned. We are all very proud of being members of the British commonwealth of nations. We hear a great deal, we read a great deal, especially in recent months, about the growing understanding, the awareness and power of those who may not be of the same colour as most of us in Canada and all of us except one in this House of Commons. The real strength of the commonwealth, Mr. Chairman, lies in the fact that there shall never be a religious nor a colour bar. The fact still remains, however, that Canada, even within the commonwealth of nations, maintains a colour bar.
I should like to ask the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, does not the maintenance of the commonwealth mean the removal, so far as immigration is concerned, of a colour bar? If we are members of the commonwealth, we are members of the commonwealth irrespective of our colour, whether we be white, black or yellow.
But the situation is still the same even under the minister. From what she has said so often from this side of the house I know of her belief in equality in commonwealth citizenship and understanding. As yet, however, she has given no indication of a change in the situation. It has been unfortunate that Canada has been held up to a bit of stigma and ridicule relative to Jamaicans and others of that type. If it is not possible nor practical to have any wide open immigration from all countries of the commonwealth, we in this group sincerely hope that the minister will be able to announce at least serious consideration of a greater honesty on behalf of Canada with respect to the landing permits for entry into our country required from those peoples who are part of the commonwealth, irrespective of their colour.
May I also state at this time that basically we are in complete agreement with her, on a planned immigration policy, as mentioned in her brief announcement when her estimates were up for consideration a week ago. We in this group have always stood for a planned immigration policy. Although we welcome immigration, it must be on a planned

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration basis and on a basis of understanding, whereby the immigrants are taken care of, because of previous commitments, and there is employment and housing for them and so that, when they come in as immigrants there is not an automatic displacement of our own Canadian citizens. May I say something to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. This may not be a completely popular thing to say but I believe it is something that must be said. In a planned immigration policy whereby, most likely on a humanitarian basis, certain provisions are made for those of non-British stock, cannot similar consideration be given to the assistance and maintenance of those who are of British stock?
I am certain that no one in this committee would express any regrets at the $14.5 million expended on behalf of the Hungarians. But, Mr. Chairman, admitting that-we voted for it-we say this. If this government is prepared to continue to spend money for their maintenance, why should not the same policy be adopted with respect to those who come from the United Kingdom? If we are prepared to pay, as we are now doing, not only the entire cost of transportation of the refugees but of their maintenance and education-and I may say that we are happy to do it-I ask the minister whether we do not owe the same consideration not only to those who come from the United Kingdom but to those of our own people who would like to be maintained in universities?
I hope that I am making it completely clear that we have never objected and do not now object to what was done. But what we say is this. How about thinking of our own people and their cost of education and how about thinking of our immigrants from the United Kingdom and their needs? There has never been one iota of assistance given in the directions which I now mention. We think it is time that the government made provision for such assistance.
I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration what consideration she is now giving or has given, or what change she may have in mind, with respect to the removal of a most iniquitous and vicious section of the regulations under the Immigration Act dealing with Canadian citizens of Chinese origin being able to bring their parents into Canada.

of Northern Affairs and National
Resources):
1.	Yes.
2.	(a) Under authority of the treasury board, the contract with Mr. Gabus, one of Europe's leading museologists, provided for a maximum payment of $5,000 during the period March 25, 1958 to March 24, 1959 inclusive. Payment was based on a rate of $100 per month plus $40 per day and travelling expenses for each day he was required to be away from home in connection with this assignment. He recommended that storage facilities should be expanded and provided with proper temperature and humidity control. He also suggested that facilities for registration and cataloguing should be improved and additional staff and space provided for the educational services. He recommended the establishment of a restoration laboratory under a trained technician. Finally he proposed certain rearrangements in the exhibition halls themselves.
Mr. Gabus also dealt with some of the desirable features to be included in a future museum, namely, three additional sections for history, pioneer life and technological discoveries.
